unit.unitTitle: Media, Technology and Judging a Source
unit.unitOverview: Work out who is actually speaking in a news report, and how far the report stands from them. Restore a headline to the sentence it stands for. Unpack a chain of four nouns into ordinary words. Then weigh a source by its interest and its independence, instead of believing it or dismissing it.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account of a misread story, a media guide and a news report.
Questions: 10 about the three texts.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about reading the news, and every pattern in it is a reading skill first.

It opens with something that happens to everybody.
A figure went round three outlets in one morning, and somebody believed it because they had seen it three times.
That is exactly the wrong reason. All three had it from the same agency, and the agency had it from one unnamed official.
One source, printed three times. Repetition is not corroboration.
Corroboration means a second source that arrived independently, and two outlets repeating one agency are not independent.

The first card is the ladder of attribution, and most people have it upside down.
At the top: the minister said. A named person, on the record, and you can check it.
One rung down: an unnamed official confirmed. Somebody real spoke to the journalist. You cannot check it, but they could.
Lower: sources close to the inquiry say. Vaguer by design, because close to could mean almost anything.
Lower still: it is understood that. Nobody is named at all. The outlet is willing to print it, and that is all you know.
The bottom: there have been reports that. The outlet is reporting other outlets.
Now here is the part worth keeping.
Most readers trust it is understood more than an unnamed official, because the first sounds official and the second sounds shifty.
It is the other way round. An unnamed source is a person a journalist has spoken to and is protecting.
It is understood may rest on nobody the outlet would name even privately.
The question that sorts all five is not who says. It is whether the outlet could answer that if pressed.

The second card is headline grammar, and there are only two rules.
First, the present simple reports a finished past event. Minister resigns means the minister has resigned. It happened.
Second, a passive drops its auxiliary. Figures questioned by auditor means the figures have been questioned.
That second rule creates the ambiguity that catches people.
Two sites closed can mean two sites have been closed, by somebody, or two sites closed, by themselves.
One of those blames a person and the other blames nobody, and only the article tells you which.
And there is a thing worth knowing about who writes these. A headline is written by an editor, not by the journalist.
That is why it can claim more than the article underneath it supports, without anybody having lied.

The third card is about a kind of phrase that fills headlines and is genuinely hard.
Council flood defence funding row. Five nouns, no prepositions at all.
There is one technique and it never fails. Read it backwards.
The last noun is the head. Row. There is a row.
Then work left. Funding row: a row about funding. Defence funding row: funding for defences. Flood defence: defences against floods. Council: the council's.
A row about the council's funding for flood defences.
Notice how many prepositions you had to supply yourself. That is what the chain removed, and it is why they can be ambiguous.
School funding review could be a review of school funding, or a funding review carried out by a school. Nothing in the words tells you.

The fourth card is about the space a report gives to people who would not speak.
Declined to comment means they were asked and refused, and that refusal is itself information.
Was unavailable for comment is much weaker. It may mean one phone call at six in the evening.
Did not respond to a request means asked, and silence.
Would not be drawn on means they spoke and avoided that particular question.
And did not deny is the strongest and the most misread. It means they were asked directly and did not say no.
It is not a confirmation. Somebody may decline to deny a thing because it is true, or because they do not know, or because they are not allowed to discuss it.

The last card is five spoken markers, and they do something the written connectives cannot.
Actually corrects gently. In fact sharpens. Mind you adds a limit while leaving your point standing. Granted concedes. Frankly warns that bluntness is coming.
All five belong to speech. In a written report they read as chatty, and Unit 6's set is what you write instead.

One closing thought about judging a source, because it is easy to take the wrong lesson from all this.
A vested interest does not make somebody wrong. An agenda is a purpose, not a plot. Every account has a slant, because every account selects.
The work is weighing, not dismissing. If you set aside every interested source you will be left with almost nothing, and what remains will have an interest too.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: Three Outlets, One Source
readings.setting: Told by somebody who checked a story
readings.passageScript:
A figure went round three outlets in a morning and I believed it because I saw it three times.
That is exactly the wrong reason, and it took me an afternoon to work out why.
All three had it from the same agency, and the agency had it from one unnamed official.
So it was not three sources. It was one source, printed three times.
Corroboration means a SECOND source that arrived independently. Repetition is not corroboration.
The other thing I had misread was a headline. Figures questioned by auditor.
I took that to mean the figures were wrong. It means an auditor had asked about them.
The article, which I had not read, said the auditor's query had been answered the same week.
The headline was not false. It was written by an editor, in four words, and it could carry no more than that.
What I do now is two things and they take about a minute.
I ask who the original source was, and whether anybody reached it independently.
And I read the third paragraph, because that is usually where the qualification lives.
Granted, a minute is more than most people will spend. It is also the whole difference.

grammar.title: Sources say: the ladder of who is actually speaking
grammar.explanation:
Unit 7 taught the reporting verb that judges, and Unit 9 taught the tense
shift. Neither covers the thing a news report does most: telling you how far
it is from the person who actually spoke.
There is a ladder, and each rung means something different.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
NAMED, on the record — you can check it:
The minister said the figures were provisional.
A spokesperson for the company stated that no decision had been made.

UNNAMED, but the outlet knows who — you cannot check it, they can:
An unnamed official confirmed the figure.
One insider described the meeting as difficult.
Sources close to the inquiry say the report is complete.

NOBODY AT ALL — the sentence names no source and no outlet:
It is understood that a decision has been reached.
It is believed that two sites will close.
The report is thought to be complete.

AND THE BOTTOM RUNG — the outlet is reporting other reports:
There have been reports that ...
It has been suggested that ...

The reader's question does not change as you go down. Who says?
It just gets harder to answer, and at the bottom it cannot be answered at all.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
A report says: it is understood that two sites will close. How much do you know?
1. Who says so? The sentence does not name anybody.
2. Does the outlet know? Possibly, and it is not saying.
3. Can you check it? No, and neither can anybody else.
Answer: you know that an outlet is willing to print it, and nothing more.

grammar.title: Minister resigns: how a headline handles time
grammar.explanation:
A headline has its own grammar, and it is not the grammar of the article
underneath it. Two rules cover almost all of it, and both are worth knowing,
because misreading a headline is the commonest way to be wrong about the news.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
RULE ONE — the PRESENT SIMPLE reports a FINISHED PAST event.
Minister resigns        = the minister has resigned
Council approves plan   = the council approved it
The present tense makes it feel like now. It happened.

RULE TWO — the passive DROPS its auxiliary.
Two sites closed        = two sites HAVE BEEN closed
Figures questioned      = the figures HAVE BEEN questioned
This is the ambiguous one. Two sites closed could also be past simple active,
meaning the sites closed themselves. The article decides which.

AND THE REST:
TO + verb means the future:   Minister to resign
-ING alone means in progress: Talks continuing
Articles disappear:           Minister resigns over pay row
The verb be disappears:       Minister under pressure

A headline is written by an editor, not by the journalist. That is why it
can claim more than the article supports.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
What does this headline actually claim? Figures questioned by auditor.
1. There is no auxiliary. Rule two says the passive has dropped one.
2. Put it back: figures HAVE BEEN questioned by an auditor.
3. So the event has happened, and an auditor did the questioning.
Answer: an auditor has questioned the figures.
Not that the figures are doubtful. Not that they are wrong. Only that
somebody has raised a question about them.
grammar.commonMistake:
The dropped auxiliary makes a passive look like an active past simple.
Two sites closed can mean two sites have been closed, or two sites closed
themselves. The first blames somebody; the second blames nobody.
Only the article tells you which. That is the reason to read it.
grammar.memoryTip: Present simple means it happened. A missing auxiliary usually means a passive.

grammar.answerKey:
1. The minister has resigned.  2. The council has approved the plan.
3. An auditor has questioned the figures.  4. The minister is going to resign.
5. Talks are continuing.  6. Two sites have been closed.
7. Number 6. It could be a passive (somebody closed them) or a past simple
   active (they closed). One blames somebody; the other blames nobody.
8. An editor, not the journalist. That is why it can claim more than the
   article supports.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Council flood defence funding row: reading a chain backwards
grammar.explanation:
Unit 4 built a noun phrase and Unit 12 chained two nouns together.
A headline chains four or five, with no prepositions at all, and the result
is dense to the point of being a puzzle.
There is one technique, and it works every time.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
READ IT BACKWARDS. The LAST noun is the head. Everything before it
describes it, and you unpack from the right.

council flood defence funding row
  row                          <- the head: there is a row
  funding row                  <- a row about funding
  defence funding row          <- funding for defences
  flood defence funding row    <- defences against floods
  council flood defence ...    <- the council's
= a row about the council's funding for flood defences

Another:
hospital waiting list figures
  figures -> list figures -> waiting list figures -> hospital ...
= figures for hospital waiting lists

Why this matters beyond headlines: the chain hides the RELATIONSHIP.
council funding row could mean a row about funding FROM the council, or a row
about funding FOR the council. The prepositions that would tell you are gone.
Where the relationship matters, write it out.
grammar.workedExample:

1. Last noun first: figures. Somebody has figures.
2. Next one left: list figures. Figures about a list.
3. Next: waiting list figures. The list is a waiting list.
4. Next: hospital. The waiting lists are hospital ones.
Answer: figures for hospital waiting lists.
Four nouns, no prepositions, and you had to supply two of them yourself.
grammar.commonMistake:
The chain can be read more than one way, and nothing in it tells you which.
school funding review could be a review of school funding, or a funding
review carried out by a school.
If your reader cannot afford to guess, use the prepositions.

grammar.title: Declined to comment: reporting what nobody would say
grammar.explanation:
Unit 9 taught you to report what people said. A news report spends almost as
much space on what people would NOT say, and those phrases are not
interchangeable. Each one describes a different event.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
DECLINED TO COMMENT = they were asked and refused.
  The company declined to comment.
  This tells you the outlet asked, and the refusal is itself information.

WAS UNAVAILABLE FOR COMMENT = the outlet could not reach them.
  The minister was unavailable for comment.
  Weaker. It may mean one telephone call at six in the evening.

DID NOT RESPOND TO A REQUEST = asked, and silence.
  The supplier did not respond to a request for comment.

WOULD NOT BE DRAWN ON = they spoke, and avoided that question.
  She would not be drawn on the timing.

DID NOT DENY = they were asked directly and did not say no.
  He did not deny that talks had taken place.
  This is the strongest of them, and the most easily misread.

Watch that last one. Did not deny is not the same as confirmed. It reports a
silence, and a silence can mean several things.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
A report says: the minister did not deny that talks had taken place.
What has the reader been told?
1. Was the minister asked? Yes — you cannot fail to deny something you were
   never asked about.
2. Did the minister confirm it? No. The sentence would say so.
3. So what happened? They were asked, and they did not say no.
Answer: a direct question was put and was not refused.
That is genuinely informative, and it is not a confirmation.
grammar.commonMistake:
did not deny reads as confirmed, and it is not.
Somebody may decline to deny a thing because it is true, because they do not
know, or because they are not permitted to discuss it.
The sentence reports only that they did not say no.
grammar.memoryTip: Each phrase reports a different event. Ask what actually happened.

2. The outlet could not reach them.
3. They were asked and said nothing.
4. They spoke, but avoided that question.
5. They were asked directly and did not say no.
6. Number 2. It may mean one call at an awkward hour.
7. No. It reports a silence, and a silence has several possible reasons.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Actually, mind you, granted: steering mid-sentence
grammar.explanation:
Unit 6 gave you the connectives of written argument. These are the spoken
equivalents, and they do something the written ones cannot: they adjust what
you have just said, without taking it back and without starting again.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
CORRECTING GENTLY:
Actually, the figure was lower than that.
actually softens a correction almost to the point of an apology.

STRENGTHENING:
The claim was weak. In fact, it was uncorroborated.
in fact usually sharpens what came before.

QUALIFYING WITHOUT RETREATING:
It was well reported. Mind you, only for two days.
mind you adds a but, and keeps the first half standing.

CONCEDING BEFORE ARGUING ON:
Granted, the source was unnamed. It was still checked.
granted does in speech what admittedly does in writing.

WARNING THAT BLUNTNESS IS COMING:
Frankly, the coverage was thin.
frankly softens and strengthens at once: it apologises in advance.

All five are SPOKEN. In a report they read as chatty. Unit 6's set — however,
nevertheless, admittedly — is what you write instead.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Somebody says the coverage was excellent. You think it was heavy but brief,
and you do not want an argument.
1. Do you disagree outright? No. The first half is true.
2. You want to keep it standing and add a limit.
3. That is mind you, which adds a but without withdrawing anything.
Answer: It was well reported. Mind you, only for two days.
Actually, it was only two days would correct them, which is a different move.
grammar.commonMistake:
These are spoken markers, and learners who have just met them put them in reports.
Weak in writing: Frankly, the coverage was thin. Mind you, it was heavy at first.
Better in writing: The coverage was thin, though heavy at first.
Keep them for speech, where they do real work.
grammar.memoryTip: actually corrects. in fact sharpens. mind you qualifies. granted concedes. frankly warns.

7. What would you write instead of number 4?
grammar.answerKey:

6. All five. They are spoken markers and read as chatty on the page.
7. Admittedly the source was unnamed. It was still checked.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Weigh the source
activities.instructionsAndItems:
For each situation, say whether the source should be believed, weighed or set aside,
and why. There is no automatic answer to any of them.
1. A firm's own figures about its own safety record.
2. The same claim in three outlets, all citing one agency.
3. An unnamed insider with a clear grievance against the company.
4. A named expert paid by one side, whose payment is disclosed.
5. An archive showing the same claim was made and not borne out in 2022.
activities.answerSummary:
1. Weigh. A vested interest does not make figures false, but they need
   independent checking before you rely on them.
2. One source, not three. Repetition is not corroboration.
3. Weigh. A grievance gives a motive AND often gives access. Neither cancels the other.
4. Weigh, and the disclosure is what makes that possible. A declared interest
   is easier to allow for than a hidden one.
5. Evidence against, not proof. A claim can be true the second time.
The pattern: almost nothing is set aside outright. Weighing is the work.
4 or 5 right: good.
activities.soloPath: For each, write what would have to be true for the source to be reliable.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the report
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. How many depots are reported as closing, and on whose word?
2. What has not been corroborated?
3. What did the spokesperson decline to comment on?
4. Copy the sentence containing 'did not deny' and say what it tells you.
5. Unpack the chain in the second half of the report.
6. What does the archive show, and why is it in the report?
activities.answerSummary:
1. Two, on the word of one unnamed official.
2. That a third site is under review.
3. The timing.
4. 'Asked directly whether any closures had been agreed, the spokesperson did
   not deny it.' They were asked and did not say no. Not a confirmation.
5. 'Staff pay review delays' = delays to the review of staff pay.
6. That a similar claim was made in 2022 and not borne out. It is there to
   weigh the fourth-depot report, which is on the bottom rung.
5 or 6 right: good.

assignments.title: The report, and the reading of it
assignments.instructions:
Part one. Write a news report of about 160 words about an invented story, with a
headline in headline grammar.
Use at least three rungs of the attribution ladder, one 'declined to comment',
one 'did not deny', and one noun chain of three or more nouns.
Part two. Now read your own report as a sceptical reader would. Write six lines:
what the headline claims against what the report actually says; who the original
source is; what has and has not been corroborated; who has a vested interest;
what the slant is; and what you would need in order to believe it.
Part three. Write the four-sentence correction the outlet would have to print if
the unnamed official turned out to be wrong.
Part four. Write three sentences of spoken commentary on your own story, using
granted, mind you and frankly, one each.
